title: Israel's Left and Right Agreed on the Saudi F-35 Deal. Both Asked for Compensation.
subtitle: National security collapsed a partisan divide
body_md:
Israel's political press is rarely united. Haaretz, left-liberal and persistently critical of the Netanyahu government, and the Jerusalem Post, centre-right and broadly supportive of the security establishment, occupy opposite ends of domestic Israeli commentary on nearly every issue. On the US State Department's September 18 approval of a potential $24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35 stealth jets to Saudi Arabia, they converged entirely.

[Haaretz](https://www.haaretz.com/middle-east-news/2026-09-18/ty-article/u-s-clears-way-for-24-3-billion-f-35-sale-to-saudi-arabia/000001a0-b0a9-df5b-adf2-f6ed909b0000) reported: "The deal has raised concerns in Israel over its regional air superiority, while Netanyahu's office says understandings with Washington will preserve Israel's edge. Senior Israeli defense officials warned the jets could expose Israeli capabilities." [Jerusalem Post](https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/defense-news/article-909029) went further: "A source told Walla that the IDF would prefer that no other country in the Middle East receive the stealth fighter, in order to preserve Israel's qualitative operational advantage" and "Israel will seek to purchase new weapons systems from US as compensation for Saudi F-35 sale."

The partisan divide collapsed because both outlets frame the question identically: not whether the sale should happen, but what Israel extracts in return. Haaretz notes Netanyahu's office has already secured "understandings" with Washington. The Jerusalem Post treats the sale as decided and pivots entirely to the compensation demand. Despite their opposing stances on almost every other question in Israeli politics, both presuppose that the deal will proceed and position Israeli security in the aftermath.

Nineteen other outlets in this 14-country corpus read the story through a different lens entirely. [AFP / France 24](https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/20260918-us-approves-24-3-billion-sale-of-48-f-35-warplanes-to-saudi-arabia) set the standard wire framing: "The United States on Thursday said it had approved a $24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35 stealth warplanes to Saudi Arabia." Most Western coverage treated the approval as a diplomatic-arms story with Israeli complications attached.

Two outliers positioned the sale inside a very different frame. Pakistan's [Dawn](https://www.dawn.com/news/2030730/us-approves-sale-of-48-f-35-jets-to-saudi-arabia) described it as "the latest major arms purchase by Riyadh since the start of the Iran war" — placing a Pentagon procurement announcement inside an active armed conflict. Malaysia's [Malay Mail](https://www.malaymail.com/news/world/2026/09/18/us-clears-us243b-sale-of-48-f35-jets-to-saudi-arabia-amid-iran-war/235618) ran the same framing, headlining "US clears US$24.3b sale of 48 F-35 jets to Saudi Arabia amid Iran war." Southeast Asian and South Asian outlets consistently foregrounded the Iran-war backdrop that every Western outlet omitted from its framing. The difference is material: a routine procurement cycle and a wartime arms shift carry different implications for regional stability.

France's AFP French-language feed surfaced a congressional dimension absent from its own English wire: French-language coverage noted that US legislators "s'inquiètent notamment que la technologie de l'appareil ne fuite vers la Chine" — worried the aircraft's technology could leak to China. This nonproliferation concern, significant for F-35 technology policy, appeared in the French feed and nowhere else in the corpus. [BBC World](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3x2zrn01pxko?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss) was the only outlet to lead with framing the story as contested rather than settled: "Why US plan to sell F-35 warplanes to Saudi Arabia is controversial," noting Saudi Arabia had "lobbied the US for years."

[Straits Times](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/us-clears-way-for-24-3-billion-fighter-jet-sale-to-saudi-arabia) reported the package value as $30.9 billion rather than the $24.3 billion cited by all other outlets — suggesting the Singapore paper's sourcing captured additional support contracts, munitions, or training beyond the base aircraft price. The gap between the two figures was not explained or reconciled in any outlet's coverage.

Two absences shape what global audiences received. No US domestic outlet appears in this cluster — the State Department announcement was made in Washington, but American press apparently processed it in separate clusters tied to congressional reaction or arms-industry coverage. No Arab or Gulf-state outlet appears despite the sale directly reshaping Gulf security balance. The regional powers most immediately affected by Saudi Arabia acquiring F-35 stealth capability — including Iran, UAE, and Egypt — have no press voice in this corpus at all.
